utterances.text: I asked to establish contact with my command in Novi Travnik, and I did not establish it. Then I sought to establish contact with Vitez, and I got it, and it is from them I think I heard that Ahmici was on fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you be more specific? Who was in Vitez, who lived in Vitez and was able to give you information on what had happened?

utterances.speaker: ANTO RAJIC
utterances.text: Well, my command was in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you be more specific? What is the name of the individual who gave you radio information at your request and who told you that Ahmici was burning?

utterances.speaker: ANTO RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Mirko Safradin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his position? What was his rank?

utterances.speaker: ANTO RAJIC
utterances.text: He was a member of the signals unit. I don't think he had a rank.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where he had this information from?

utterances.speaker: ANTO RAJIC
utterances.text: I never managed to ask him. That was all I heard, and then I lost contact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us what time you had this radio contact with him?

utterances.speaker: ANTO RAJIC
utterances.text: Around 9.30 in the morning on the 16th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you be as specific as possible as to what Mirko Safradin told you on the 16th of April, 1993, around 9.00 in the morning?

utterances.speaker: ANTO RAJIC
utterances.text: Well, the whole conversation lasted not more than 20 seconds. I did not know what was going on. I didn't even know that there was shooting going on, because we could not hear. I asked him if there was anything he knew down there, and he told me, "Anto, Ahmici is on fire." Then he started another sentence, and the line went off.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he mention any victims?

utterances.speaker: ANTO RAJIC
utterances.text: No, no, he did not mention, because nothing was known yet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If there is an idea that Ahmici is on fire, does that not necessarily imply that there are victims?

utterances.speaker: ANTO RAJIC
utterances.text: Well, it can be, but need not be. I mean, he did not have to know about this, anything, at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us try to be as clear as possible, Mr. Rajic. You're telling us that in the morning of the 16th of April, the transmission service of the PZO in Vitez knows and tells you that Ahmici is burning?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: If I got it right, the witness mentioned 9.00 -- 9.30. You keep saying 9.00, but he says 9.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: A little bit earlier up, he said -- you're right. You're right. You're right. I apologise for this. I made the mistake.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to put the question to you again, Mr. Rajic, in a more precise way. You tell us that around 9.30 in the morning on the 16th of April, 1993, the transmission services of PZO in Vitez knew that Ahmici was on fire?

utterances.speaker: ANTO RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said previously that when you heard this, you tried to establish telephone contact with your wife, with your family. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: ANTO RAJIC
utterances.text: Correct, but that was right before the dusk fell, because the radio connection was already dead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, did the telephone keep working? Could you have proper telephone contact with Ahmici during all those days?

utterances.speaker: ANTO RAJIC
utterances.text: With Ahmici, no -- I mean with Santici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Santici. I see.

utterances.speaker: ANTO RAJIC
utterances.text: That evening, that conversation with my wife, and that evening, telephones also went dead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that on the 18th of April, by then you had taken position at Zabilje, and you watched television. Could you tell us what time you watched television, or for which period of time, starting when and finishing when?

utterances.speaker: ANTO RAJIC
utterances.text: 19.00, 19.30, that is when the prime time news of the Bosnian -- or rather, to be more exact, Sarajevo television, and the news went on until 20.00. Of course, it lasted longer because of all those reports.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you sure that you watched TV Sarajevo, Mr. Rajic?

utterances.speaker: ANTO RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Sarajevo television. It is their news programme, but that programme included footage of various foreign televisions, CNN and other companies. I wouldn't know which ones. That is, I don't know what they are called.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember seeing the logo of TV Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ANTO RAJIC
utterances.text: That was the only television which could work at that time. At that time, only BH TV was possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In respect of the Ahmici event as reported in the evening of the 18th of April by that TV station, do you remember whether other people than [redacted] were asked to express their views?

utterances.speaker: ANTO RAJIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, there were other people who were interviewed, but I don't know the names of these persons. I don't know [redacted] either, at that time, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you confirm to us -- you have actually already done so just now -- but that at the time you didn't know at all who [redacted] was, or at least the one we have in mind?

utterances.speaker: ANTO RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I didn't know him at all. I knew the name, but I didn't know the man, that man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us who else expressed themselves on the television on that TV channel about the events in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: ANTO RAJIC
utterances.text: You mean persons from Ahmici, or generally speaking?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The people in Ahmici, but you seem to remember that very exactly, very vividly. You seem to remember what [redacted] said very clearly, what he said on the 18th of April, 1993, on TV Sarajevo. I'm asking you, and I think you are in a position to tell us, who else spoke about the events on that same TV channel?

utterances.speaker: ANTO RAJIC
utterances.text: There were other persons, but I don't know them, as I told you. A woman spoke, but I don't know who she was. An elderly woman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recollect what that elderly woman said then?

utterances.speaker: ANTO RAJIC
utterances.text: Similar to [redacted], that the village was on fire. That was the first statement she made. And then [redacted] spoke a bit more, because she was crying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any recollection of other people yet?

utterances.speaker: ANTO RAJIC
utterances.text: From Ahmici? No. No. No, I can't remember. How could I remember everything now?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To be quite clear, apart from what [redacted] [redacted] said, you remember an elderly woman who was crying and saying that Ahmici was on fire, and that is all? Is that so?

utterances.speaker: ANTO RAJIC
utterances.text: That's all, because [redacted] spoke the most, so that is how I remember his statement the best.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you have a very vivid recollection of him, although you didn't know him, whilst you have only a very dim memory as to the other people who might have spoken on that programme; am I reflecting your words or thoughts correctly in saying so?

utterances.speaker: ANTO RAJIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, you have reflected it well. But [redacted] spoke at length, and this woman was crying. She hardly finished her sentence properly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At any rate, she didn't say anything that would have struck you in any way? Mr. Rajic, when did you see that programme again, that cassette again?

utterances.speaker: ANTO RAJIC
utterances.text: You mean the recording from the Zenica hospital? On video? No, I never saw that on video.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean that you never watched it again, is that so, until today?

utterances.speaker: ANTO RAJIC
utterances.text: Today I did, yes, but never before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you 100 per cent sure that that TV programme was broadcast on the 18th?

utterances.speaker: ANTO RAJIC
utterances.text: I think it was the 18th. 99 per cent, I'm sure that it was the 18th. Possibly it was the 19th, but I think it was the 18th. Because it was the same night when we arrived there at Pokrajcici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What day of the week was it?

utterances.speaker: ANTO RAJIC
utterances.text: I can't say now. I know that the 16th was a Friday, the 17th was Saturday. Sunday? Sunday? I'm sure you'll be able to do your sums.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to you, Mr. Rajic, since [redacted] [redacted] was admitted into hospital at 5.00 on the 16th of April, what was his physical and mental condition the next day?

utterances.speaker: ANTO RAJIC
utterances.text: Well, judging by the looks of him, he was psychologically able to give an interview.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think that the Prosecutor is really crossing the line now, because he is asking the witness to draw certain conclusions about certain facts that he has no idea of. He is not in a position to say what kind of a condition a person may be a day after he was hurt, so I think the Prosecutor is not entitled to ask that kind of a question of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I admit that Mr. Rajic is not in a good position to answer that question, but the reason why I was asking it is that he said before that if he knew who it was who killed his family, he should have told everybody viewing the programme, and that's in view of that piece of information, which I thought was very bold, given the state of knowledge of Mr. Rajic. That's why I asked the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I see. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One last question, Mr. Rajic. On the 18th of April -- I'm talking about daytime on the 18th of April -- the conflict as it was named between the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the HVO started?

utterances.speaker: ANTO RAJIC
utterances.text: On the 18th?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ANTO RAJIC
utterances.text: The conflict started on the 16th -- well, yes, yes, on the 18th. That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is under way, then, the 18th. Is it right to say that on the 18th of April, the outcome of the conflict is totally unknown?

utterances.speaker: ANTO RAJIC
utterances.text: The position where I was, it was impossible to tell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that day, it is not possible to know what is going to become of the Lasva Valley and of the inhabitants thereof?

utterances.speaker: ANTO RAJIC
utterances.text: Impossible. I couldn't know a thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [redacted] couldn't know either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: That's a comment, if I may say so, Mr. Terrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: It is, but I have no further questions of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mrs. Slokovic-Glumac, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Re-examined by Ms. Slokovic-Glumac:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rajic, very briefly, could you please tell us, what are all the things you did in order to try to get hold of the videotape of what you saw on the 18th?

utterances.speaker: ANTO RAJIC
utterances.text: I did all sorts of things. I looked all over, Germany, the Netherlands, Austria, because I recall his statement 100 per cent, but I can't prove it without the cassette itself. So what is most reliable is my own statement, and then to be followed by the videocassette. And what I'm saying now is the truth, 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you just tell us the following: Until the present day, you have not seen this video cassette. That is to say that in the previous period, before you made this statement that we submitted to the court, you had not seen this cassette?

utterances.speaker: ANTO RAJIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What you recall is only from this single viewing, that time at that position in Pokrajcici?

utterances.speaker: ANTO RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Please tell us, this man who you established contact with in Vitez, he worked as a signals man in the command at the headquarters of what brigade?

utterances.speaker: ANTO RAJIC
utterances.text: That is to say, the command of the PZO, my anti-aircraft defence. Please, I want to correct one thing. Mirko Safradin is this signals man, and he is the next witness, I mean, lest there be any misunderstanding. I want to say of this my own free will.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So Mirko Safradin, who worked at this PZO station in Vitez is not the same person?

utterances.speaker: ANTO RAJIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. No, Mirko Safradin, the one who established contact with me, he was killed at Buhine Kuce, as a civilian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, this station, RUP 12, is that a military station? Is it part of some military equipment that exists in the organisation?

utterances.speaker: ANTO RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. RUP 12 is a radio station of the former Yugoslav People's Army that we had before all of this. As far as I can remember, it was there from '78, although I had one in the army in the JNA too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With this transmitter RUP 12, can an amateur also have it and use it at home or is this a military transmitter that not everyone can have and can only be obtained from the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ANTO RAJIC
utterances.text: Well, when the JNA fell apart everybody could have got it, that's a fact, but a unit could also get it as a unit, because at that time when the Serbs were withdrawing people took things away. So whoever took anything away would keep it. Although it is an expensive transmitter, and I don't think an individual could really own it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So a military structure could have that kind of a transmitter; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The village guards that were in Santici, for example, did they have radios?

utterances.speaker: ANTO RAJIC
utterances.text: No. No, they didn't even have a rifle, let alone a radio.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm talking about the Croats in Santici. Did they have a radio station?

utterances.speaker: ANTO RAJIC
utterances.text: No. No. Again, I'm telling you, it's not guards, it's patrols.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether in Santici, Pirici they had some other guard, some other part of the village that was also held by the Croats with some kind of guards? Did these other parts perhaps have an RUP 12?

utterances.speaker: ANTO RAJIC
utterances.text: Nobody can have an RUP 12 except for a strong military unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Did you know that the Muslims in Ahmici had an RUP 12 at the school?

utterances.speaker: ANTO RAJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. All right. Tell me, this anti-aircraft gun that you were manning, what was its range?

utterances.speaker: ANTO RAJIC
utterances.text: Well, its range was from 8.5 to 9 kilometres, with an armoured shell. The other anti-aircraft shell would explode earlier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So from your position you could not really fire at any of the areas that were in a state of war on the 16th.

utterances.speaker: ANTO RAJIC
utterances.text: No. No, we couldn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me one more thing. You probably know Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic well. Could you tell me what you talked about to them and what their interests were?

utterances.speaker: ANTO RAJIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you talk about with Mirjan and Zoran Kupreskic? What did they say in terms of politics? What were their thoughts?

utterances.speaker: ANTO RAJIC
utterances.text: They were strongly opposed to what was going on. They were against this policy that was waged from 1992. At any rate, somebody above them and somebody who was above us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were they like? Were they in favour of war, in favour of a war option, or were they people who led normal and peaceful lives? Would you tell us, please?

utterances.speaker: ANTO RAJIC
utterances.text: These were people who led normal and peaceful lives. Zoran is an intellectual. He's a mechanical engineer. During the first conflict he tried to pacify everyone. There is no theoretical chance of them being advocates of anything like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Rajic, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: I have concluded my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, there is a whole series of questions that was asked by my learned friend during her new in chief which did not seem, to me, to be within the limits of the cross-examination. I think -- I believe that all these questions regarding one's political options are simply --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. I was about to ask Mrs. Slokovic-Glumac not to address that question. We fully agree with you. In the future, I think that the counsel for Defence should limit themselves to only additional questions rather than new questions which go beyond the cross-examination or, if necessary, perhaps to go deeper into a matter that was raised in chief but not something else. So that applies for the future. We don't have any further questions for the witness. Mr. Rajic, thank you for giving evidence in court. You may now be released. The witness is being released. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I apologise, but I would like to go back for one minute to the exhibits concerning witness Mirko Vidovic. For the sake of propriety, I would like to suggest that the Exhibit D28/3 should only relate to the permit, because now we are aware that there were two different documents that were photocopied on one page. So I would suggest that the small document, which is now by itself, be given the number D28A/3. I would also like to suggest that the photocopy which is D29/3 should be replaced by a photocopy, made by the Registry, of the whole passport, so that the photocopy would be handed to both the Prosecution and Defence counsel. We will keep the original in the Registry file, and I think it is only proper for Defence counsel and the Prosecution to have a photocopy of the whole document for the purpose of future examination or cross-examination of other witnesses or for the closing statements. These are minor things but I thought it would be necessary. I apologise for being so slow in reflecting on this matter. We could now call witness Taraba, Mr. Taraba. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Taraba. Could you please make the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down. Counsel Radovic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Radovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good day, Mr. Taraba.

utterances.speaker: IVAN TARABA
utterances.text: Good day to you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you introduce yourself for the Court? That is, give us your name, your father's name, your date of birth, and your address.

utterances.speaker: IVAN TARABA
utterances.text: I'm Ivan Taraba. My father's name is Marko. I was born on the 2nd of December, 1941 in Vitez. My address is Kralja Petra Kresimira Cetritog number 1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, in 1992 and in 1993, who did you live with?

utterances.speaker: IVAN TARABA
utterances.text: With my family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your family consisted of?

utterances.speaker: IVAN TARABA
utterances.text: Of my wife, my son, daughter, and mother.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, where did your mother live?

utterances.speaker: IVAN TARABA
utterances.text: At that time she lived in the country, in my weekend cottage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the name of this village where your mother lived?

utterances.speaker: IVAN TARABA
utterances.text: Jardol.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you often visit your mother in the village of Jardol?

utterances.speaker: IVAN TARABA
utterances.text: Almost every day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, in 1992 and 1993, where did you work?

utterances.speaker: IVAN TARABA
utterances.text: I worked in the Slobodan Princip Seljo company in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did that factory mean for the town of Vitez from an economic point of view in relation to the population of Vitez? Could you explain this a bit? Could you dwell on it a bit more, because you're familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: IVAN TARABA
utterances.text: It meant a great deal. It is a factory that made products that belonged to the special purposes industry, that is to say, for the Yugoslav People's Army. It was one of the largest companies in Vitez, and it was broadly linked to various companies throughout the former Yugoslavia. It also meant a great deal to the town of Vitez and the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did it have many people who were employed there at this factory?

utterances.speaker: IVAN TARABA
utterances.text: Well, almost 1.000 workers. I don't know the exact figure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, what are you by profession?

utterances.speaker: IVAN TARABA
utterances.text: I am a mechanical engineer, with a university degree.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, how did your career evolve? I'm actually interested in the part that pertains to your employment in the factory, that is to say, when you first started working in the factory and throughout that period until 1992 and 1993.

utterances.speaker: IVAN TARABA
utterances.text: Practically I worked in that factory from 1962. In '92 and '93, I had a job that I originally got in 1985.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what job is this?

utterances.speaker: IVAN TARABA
utterances.text: I was head of maintenance of special -- of the special purpose industry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know Mirjan Kupreskic?

utterances.speaker: IVAN TARABA
utterances.text: I knew Mirjan as an inhabitant of the town of Vitez and as a worker who was employed at the site where the former Unis factories were. That is to say, in other words, I knew him personally. I knew where he worked and I knew what he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But did you know him well or just like that, superficially? How should I put this?

utterances.speaker: IVAN TARABA
utterances.text: Well, superficially, because he was at the same site. We went to the same cafeteria. We saw each other every day, but we didn't meet through work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know Zoran Kupreskic?

utterances.speaker: IVAN TARABA
utterances.text: I know Zoran very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How come?

utterances.speaker: IVAN TARABA
utterances.text: Well, we are colleagues. We're involved in the same line of work. I was also his immediate supervisor for a certain period of time when I was transferred to the special purpose industry, rather, to the Slobodan Princip Seljo enterprise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, in this enterprise in 1992 and 1993, that is to say, until the outbreak of the war -- I'm really interested in the period up to the 15th of April, 1993. What was the ethnic composition of the employees in this company?

utterances.speaker: IVAN TARABA
utterances.text: Well, as far as these factories are concerned, there were about 3.500 workers. The ethnic composition was a balanced one in line with the ethnic composition of the population of the municipality of Vitez. The same goes for that part of the factory in which I worked in 1992, 1993, in which Mr. Kupreskic worked in as well or, rather, in our own department, the one that I headed and where Mr. Zoran Kupreskic was subordinated to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So tell me, what would the proportions be, roughly?

utterances.speaker: IVAN TARABA
utterances.text: Out of the 28 employees in our organisational unit, there were about 50 per cent Croats, that is to say, Croats and Muslims, and a few Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, after the first free elections and after the government was established as a result of these elections, was there any discrimination within this enterprise against any ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: IVAN TARABA
utterances.text: Well, I assert that one cannot speak of discrimination in this environment where I was fully aware of the ethnic composition, of the relations between the employees, and specifically in terms of action taken both by myself as supervisor or by my subordinates.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you also aware of developments beyond your department?

utterances.speaker: IVAN TARABA
utterances.text: No. What we did, Mr. Kupreskic and I, was rather specific.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is so specific about it? Could you describe it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN TARABA
utterances.text: This is military production. That's what's specific. That production always required greater responsibility than in other places. One had to be punctual; responsible; conscientious, may I say; and that particular environment was always spared of various developments that took place outside and around that environment. So we were quite apart from these developments that took place. We were required to keep production going at all times. That is why we were quite isolated from these external developments.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1990-'92 or 1993, did the production drop and, thus, a number of redundant workers appeared?

utterances.speaker: IVAN TARABA
utterances.text: I could hardly answer that question. I think that, generally speaking, the production declined, but at the place where I worked, this decline did not mean that employees were given notice because our task was a specific one. If the production stopped, then we would go into overhaul, into maintenance, replacement of parts, and maintenance of a number of installations so all the equipment would be ready for work at any time. So that it would happen, for instance, if all the production workers were on holidays, every other worker was on holidays or whatever, laid off. We worked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But did it ever happen in '92 or '93 that Zoran was laid off or did not come to work?

utterances.speaker: IVAN TARABA
utterances.text: All I remember is that in 1992, sometime June, we were all kind of laid off for about three weeks or perhaps 20 days, and that was the only interruption we had. That is a time of summer holidays, so that we were all absent at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Otherwise, he always came to work regularly, or was he absent frequently, or did he come to work regularly?

utterances.speaker: IVAN TARABA
utterances.text: Mr. Zoran was the head for machine maintenance, and he always had to be there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, that is all right, but was he always?

utterances.speaker: IVAN TARABA
utterances.text: Yes, he was always there. He was regularly there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the days right before the war, that is, 15th of April? Was he at work then?

utterances.speaker: IVAN TARABA
utterances.text: I remember that very well because that day Zoran and I left the company -- came out of the company together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you went where?

utterances.speaker: IVAN TARABA
utterances.text: We went towards our locality in Vitez. We walked. We went on foot to Vitez with another gentleman, of Muslim origin, who also worked in our company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You being Zoran's boss, did you happen to notice his attitude to those people subordinated to him? Did he distinguish between Croats and Muslims and, thus, did he harass Muslims or did he apply a balance to both groups?

utterances.speaker: IVAN TARABA
utterances.text: Zoran had 28 workers under him. Mechanical, that is. Machine operators, that is. As his head, I know that Zoran had a very correct attitude towards all of them, but Zoran is such as a person. I mean, he does not make a distinction according to one's ethnic origin. If you will allow me to add something, I have an example, an instance, of a very humane, of a very warm-hearted attitude towards a subordinate who was a Muslim. Zoran and I sometimes would start discussing why he wasn't at work, because that particular machine operator had a father who was a diabetic -- a diabetes patient, and he, therefore, was frequently absent because of his father's absence. Now, Zoran was -- Zoran put up with that. I man, he was quite tolerant. That particular machine operator was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember his name?

utterances.speaker: IVAN TARABA
utterances.text: Yes, of course, very well. His name was Nermin Ahmic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you perhaps know the names of people he mostly socialised with, he was closest with, within the factory?

utterances.speaker: IVAN TARABA
utterances.text: Well, I could give you some names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So will you please do it, only will you please, when you say a name, tell us what the ethnicity of that person is.

utterances.speaker: IVAN TARABA
utterances.text: Zoran directly cooperated, worked, and sat in the office, day in and day out, with -- or rather partook of coffee day in and day out with the head of the production unit, Mr. Mahmutovic; with an electric technician, Senad Topoljak; with the production overseer, Dragan Grebenar; with our tools operator, Ivan Josipovic; and if I may, with the floor manager, Tarahija, who is a Muslim. On the team there were no Serbs, because those couple of Serb bosses were directly in the production plant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, but tell us, do you know what was the specific job of Zoran's in the winter of 1992 and in nineteen-ninety ...

utterances.speaker: IVAN TARABA
utterances.text: Yes, I do know it very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So will you tell us?

utterances.speaker: IVAN TARABA
utterances.text: Zoran, that is, I, as his superior, as the head of that service, we had three separate entities for special purposes production, and Mr. Zoran, as the production was reduced before the winter came, his task was, together with our Muslim colleague, to prepare plant units for the winter season, primarily with a view to preventing the freezing of equipment, to avoid damage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Until when was he engaged in this?

utterances.speaker: IVAN TARABA
utterances.text: I could not tell you exactly until what date he was committed to that, but it must have been until the time of low temperatures, until such time when water begins to freeze.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you listed the names that Zoran socialised with within the company, you did not tell us what their ethnic origin was. So will you please repeat those names, and every time tell us also what the ethnic origin was of that person.

utterances.speaker: IVAN TARABA
utterances.text: Mr. Mahmutovic, as the chief of chemical workers, was Muslim; Mr. Tarahija was also of Muslim origin; Mr. Grabovac (sic), a Croat; Mr. Josipovic -- rather, sorry, not Grabovac; Grebenar, I'm sorry, Grebenar -- a Croat; Mr. Josipovic, a Croat; Mr. Topoljak, a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us if there was any written record of when who came for work, and how.

utterances.speaker: IVAN TARABA
utterances.text: We regularly recorded it. There was a log of daily attendance at work, that is, the presence or absence of every employee. Briefly, we had a shift log. That is what we had, a shift log.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who kept this log?

utterances.speaker: IVAN TARABA
utterances.text: The shift log was with the head of the mechanical maintenance department, Mr. Kupreskic, and the second logbook was with the head of the electrical maintenance unit, Mr. --just wait a moment -- Stipe Stipinovic. If I may add, both those gentlemen and Mr. Topoljak shared the office, and they each kept a separate shift log.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where these logs are kept now?

utterances.speaker: IVAN TARABA
utterances.text: No, it is not known where these logs are, because the offices were ravaged, and a lot of documentation was destroyed or taken away, or in other words stolen, because since our withdrawal, or since our departure from the company on the 15th, that is, on the eve of the conflict, we simply did not enter the company, so anyone who passed by could enter it. It was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But tell us, apart from business contacts, did you talk to Zoran, did you converse with Zoran about other topics? Do you know what were his interests outside work?

utterances.speaker: IVAN TARABA
utterances.text: I know Mr. Zoran very well indeed. I know his spheres of his interest, and perhaps it might be interesting to note now that Mr. Zoran likes folklore. That is his hobby.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We don't have to talk about that, because we really have heard a great deal about all this. Everybody recognises him. But apart from folklore, was there anything else?

utterances.speaker: IVAN TARABA
utterances.text: Mr. Zoran is a very sociable person, so he always attends those parties in Vitez, various festivities there. Perhaps the Court might care to know, even though this is perhaps sort of personal, Mr. Zoran is a man who is interested and is actively practising yoga and those transcendental -- how shall I put it -- issues, things. He read books on the subject, and he -- well, we're very close, and I also have a propensity for it, so we did talk about this. We exchanged views and literature and talked about these things. In Vitez there is such a circle of people interested in these things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But tell us, this Indian literature that Zoran studied, does it preach violence, or something else?

utterances.speaker: IVAN TARABA
utterances.text: I believe that all those gentlemen present here know very well what they say --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, let the present gentlemen be; tell us what it's about.

utterances.speaker: IVAN TARABA
utterances.text: Well, what I said, as my people in Bosnia say, nobody will get a headache from that literature. It's the saying over there. Mr. Zoran, perhaps thanks to that kind of literature, he would never harm an ant, is how we say in Bosnia, let alone inflict suffering or pain on anyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So to cut a long story short, this is a philosophy which preaches non-violence?

utterances.speaker: IVAN TARABA
utterances.text: Yes, definitely non-violence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think it is time to make a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. Have you many more questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do have very many of them, but on another matter altogether, not on the Hindu philosophy or anything like that. We have, as you see, skipped folklore, as you have noticed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. We will take a 15-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Radovic, so far you have dealt with issues which are covered by the witness's statement. I hope you will not go beyond those matters, Counsel Radovic. We are very keen to finish by Thursday with the five more witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: The last witness who has been envisaged for today pertains to the same circumstances as witness Rajic, and I shall be examining him, and we are going to shorten the proceedings considerably.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Taraba, please, would you continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Can I continue my questioning?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Taraba, we are continuing, and we'd like to speed things up a bit. So tell me, on the eve of the war, on the 15th of April, you went to your village; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN TARABA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you when the shooting began the next day?

utterances.speaker: IVAN TARABA
utterances.text: I was in my weekend cottage when the shooting started. I was in the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then tell us what happened with you after that, but just tell us very briefly, because we are not really all that interested in that.

utterances.speaker: IVAN TARABA
utterances.text: I stayed in the village, and I spent the entire war in the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Until when?

utterances.speaker: IVAN TARABA
utterances.text: Until the 25th of July, when I had to go to hospital because I was wounded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, this village where your mother was, and where your weekend cottage was, and where you went every day, were there village guards there?

utterances.speaker: IVAN TARABA
utterances.text: Village guards did exist. As I was passing by, going to see my relatives in the village, I would notice a group of three or four young men who were patrolling the road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, which village is this, this village of yours, is a it Croat or a Muslim village or a mixed village?

utterances.speaker: IVAN TARABA
utterances.text: It is purely Croat village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These village guards that patrolled the area, did they find something any time with anyone?

utterances.speaker: IVAN TARABA
utterances.text: Well, rumour had it that as Muslims passed through that village to their own village, through that village to their own village --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that a transit village, then?

utterances.speaker: IVAN TARABA
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Rumour had it that when they searched their vehicles, that they would find ammunition in them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The last question would be, do you remember walking on foot through the Mahala and seeing something unusual in the Mahala, something unusual, an unusual building or something?

utterances.speaker: IVAN TARABA
utterances.text: Well, it's not only that I remember it. This was quite a surprise for us, and it came as a terrible defeat to us, that there were bunkers on the outskirts of town. Zoran and I were together, and we were commenting on this: "Who are they making this bunker for?" The bunker was built overnight, and it was camouflaged, but you could see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Try to think of the time when this happened.

utterances.speaker: IVAN TARABA
utterances.text: That could have been a few days prior to the conflict.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which conflict? The first or the second one?

utterances.speaker: IVAN TARABA
utterances.text: The conflict on the 16th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is to say before the war began?

utterances.speaker: IVAN TARABA
utterances.text: Yes, before the war began, and we were commenting on the fact that this was probably built overnight by machines and then camouflaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have finished with this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I assume there is no cross-examination by other Defence counsel then? Mr. Blaxill?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. Cross-examined by Mr. Blaxill:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Taraba, good afternoon to you, sir. My name is Michael Blaxill.

utterances.speaker: IVAN TARABA
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am one of the attorneys assigned to the Prosecution in this case, and I do have just a few questions to ask you, sir, but not very many. You say that Mr. Zoran Kupreskic had worked as your subordinate for some time. Can you indicate how long that was, sir?

utterances.speaker: IVAN TARABA
utterances.text: I think it was for about four or five years. I can't tell exactly. I would have to try to remember. About four to five years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe, from your description, the work you did within your section of the factory was work of some very special importance in military production; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: IVAN TARABA
utterances.text: Very important and responsible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that work involve your being conscious of issues of security and of the secrecy of some of the work, perhaps? That kind of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: IVAN TARABA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the work involve the handling, in the production sense, of any particularly dangerous materials, where issues of safety were very paramount?

utterances.speaker: IVAN TARABA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In those circumstances, sir, I believe you've indicated that the highest standards of professional competence and discipline were required of the people working in that section, presumably for safety reasons, if nothing else.

utterances.speaker: IVAN TARABA
utterances.text: I don't really think I understood the question. Please, could you clarify it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The working practices that you needed to have in your section, and the standards of professional self-discipline of the staff, were they important for the safety of the work that you did?

utterances.speaker: IVAN TARABA
utterances.text: It was for the purpose of the technological safety of the work involved, because these were explosives, so we're talking about technological safety.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have spoken very highly of Mr. Zoran Kupreskic and his kindness to members of staff and his fair treatment of people. Would it also be fair to say that he needed to impose high standards of professional conduct and discipline as well, as well as showing compassion to his co-workers?

utterances.speaker: IVAN TARABA
utterances.text: I think that kindness could even be excluded, because Mr. Kupreskic is a person who very professionally and responsibly, without being fearful of any objections, carried out his duties together with subordinates. I think that kindness was what he exhibited when he had coffee with people, and apart from work, because this kind of work requires a great deal of conscientiousness, and also a high level of expertise and professionalism.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You say that you and Mr. Kupreskic departed from the factory on the 15th of April. By that, do you mean that you simply went home as normal? Or had you been told that there was some reason you would not be going back?

utterances.speaker: IVAN TARABA
utterances.text: No one told us that, nor did we expect not to be coming to work. This happened all of a sudden, at least for me. I don't know about others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But as far as you were concerned, you expected to go back to work, say, on the 16th, in the normal way?

utterances.speaker: IVAN TARABA
utterances.text: Yes, and no one had put his things away, his personal belongings or the things they had for working purposes. We expected to come back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You returned to the village of Jardol that evening, the evening of the 15th, to your weekend home?

utterances.speaker: IVAN TARABA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly sir, in your evidence --

utterances.speaker: IVAN TARABA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, no, no. No, no, no, no, not the weekend cottage. No, no, no, I went back to where my apartment is, and from the apartment I went to the weekend cottage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But on the night of the 15th, you did spend the night, did you, at the weekend cottage in Jardol?

utterances.speaker: IVAN TARABA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say you were awoken by the sounds of conflict the next day and, in fact, you remained in the village right up to the 25th of July, is that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: IVAN TARABA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see Mr. Zoran Kupreskic at all between the 15th of April and the 25th of July?

utterances.speaker: IVAN TARABA
utterances.text: No. No, not at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were acquainted with Mr. Mirjan Kupreskic. Did you see him at all between the 15th of April and the 25th of July?

utterances.speaker: IVAN TARABA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Counsel Radovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have no further questions after the cross-examination. I think that my previous questions were sufficient. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. We have no questions for the witness. Mr. Taraba, thank you so much for giving evidence. You may now be released.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're welcome. Thank you. (The witness withdrew) (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Would you please make the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down. Counsel Radovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, since this witness is supposed to testify to circumstances similar to those related by Anto Rajic, I shall try to shorten the proceedings as much as possible, and I shall immediately talk about the things why he was called in to testify in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Radovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Safradine, could you please introduce yourself to the Court first and tell us your name, your surname, the name of your father, your date of birth, your address?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: I'm Mirko Safradin. I was born on the 3rd of January, 1964. Franjo is my father's name. My address is Santici, 130, the municipality of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Towards the end of 1992 and until the outbreak of the war, which we consider to be the 16th of April, 1993, who did you live with?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: I have a family, a wife, and two children, and my father, and my mother.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know Anto Rajic?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: Yes. He's my neighbour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your military orientation, so to speak, what was your military duty or, rather, what was your military training, or what was the military assignment that you had?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: I was a member of the PZO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does the PZO mean?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: That is the anti-aircraft defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall, as a member of the anti-aircraft defence were you in any contact with witness DG Rajic?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: Well, I was with Anto throughout in the anti-aircraft defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember what kind of weaponry you had?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: Yes. It was a gun of 40 millimetres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the make?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: Bofors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember, in the period of the 16th of April until the 25th of April, where you were with this gun?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: We were in Pokrajcici. On the 18th we were transferred to Prahulje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This place that you were transferred to on the 18th, are you sure that that was the place or are you a bit confused with the names of the villages?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: Well, I said that first we were in Prahulje and on the 18th we were transferred to Pokrajcici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were transferred to the village of Pokrajcici, were you by your gun all the time or did you have time to relax or did you go to a house somewhere?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: Since we came in the afternoon, we had time. We sought accommodation there and things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you find accommodation?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: Yes. We met a gentleman and a lady called Jako and Luca Bilic, and they offered accommodation to us and that's where we stayed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The place where you stayed at, were you there on your own or were you with Anto Rajic?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: I was with Anto Rajic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The house that you stayed at, did it have a TV set?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do when you came to that house?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: We watched the news on television. We watched the news programme of TV Sarajevo and, naturally, we were interested in what was going on down there. In the news I recognised [redacted].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you known him from before, [redacted]?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know exactly where his house was? How well did you know him?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: I knew where his house was, and I knew him because his son went to elementary school with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which son?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: Naser.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever come to his home?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps once, not more than that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you see in this television programme where [redacted] appeared? Tell us what you remembered from this television programme.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: He was laying, half laying. His arms and hands were bandaged up to the elbows and his face were burned. He talked about some soldiers barging into his house and killing his son, his daughter-in-law, and two grandchildren.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You remember that well, did you?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Then this journalist, I don't know if it was a man or a lady journalist, but this person asked whether he had recognised the attackers. He said that he didn't recognise anyone because they were camouflaged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, did you know the hospital -- where the hospital was, the hospital where he was in?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: It said that it was the hospital in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time of this TV programme that you're talking about, who held the town of Zenica? You had civilian and military authority in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: Well, it was the Muslims. Them primarily.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, during the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, during the war between the Muslims and the Croats or when the Muslims and the Croats waged war with the Serbs, was there any danger for the town of Zenica, that is, having the Muslims lose the town of Zenica?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: Could you please repeat that question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At any point of time during the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, were the Muslims ever in danger of being expelled from Zenica, to the best of your knowledge, of course?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: Well, that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, in a military sense, did the town of Zenica have a lot of Muslim soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, because they were a majority there, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was a strong military stronghold?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember, in the news where you recognised [redacted], whether mention was made of anything else? Do you remember any other information that you heard and saw that evening on television?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: No. I only remember what I said just now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I know, but then there is the logical question of why did that draw your attention. Why did you remember that rather than other things from the news which included that detail about [redacted]?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: Well, I remember that because I knew the man from earlier on and because I was interested in what he would say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the journalist put his or her question to [redacted] as to who had done that, was that a single question or was that question repeated?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: The question was repeated once again, twice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Radovic, that is a leading question, quite obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I give up this question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now tell me, did you and Rajic comment on what you had seen on television or did you not do that?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: Well, we listened to what he had to say, and it's not that there was some --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, what [redacted] said that he did not recognise the persons who had done it, did he give an explanation why he could not recognise them?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: What I said. He did not recognise them, and he could not recognise them. Then the journalist asked him whether he recognised the persons who did it. He said, "No, I didn't because they were camouflaged." So that was repeated twice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember that either I or my colleague, Ms. Slokovic-Glumac, asked to you make a statement about what you had seen?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember whether you made a statement to us?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When we were questioning you, did we explain to you why we needed that statement of yours instead of showing the Court the entire news item that we were talking about? Did we explain this to you, what we needed it for?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, you did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why was this?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: Because [redacted], in that statement, accused Zoran and Miro Kupreskic. No? No? I didn't understand what you said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I imagine you didn't understand the question. When we talked to you, was any mention made of whether we had that cassette or were we looking for the video cassette? I'm sorry, but it's better for me to put a direct question, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: Could you please repeat what you said? I didn't understand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When we talked to you, did we tell you whether we had this cassette or we did not have this cassette with the news programme?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: You didn't have the cassette.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We didn't have the cassette. Then you told us what you saw but without seeing this video cassette?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You remembered that what you saw is what you told us about today; right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, now I would like Prosecutor's Exhibit 557 to be shown to the witness, the video.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now you will see this particular news item, and will you please watch it carefully? (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: (Voiceover) Reporter: " ... uniforms of the Croat Defence Council. There is a very moving story of [redacted] [redacted] because some creatures in uniforms from the HVO killed his son, a daughter-in-law, and two sons of whom one was in a cradle. He was only three months and three days old." [redacted]: "Yesterday, in the morning of the 16th of April, sometime around 5.00, we were still asleep then. The child was crying, because I had a grandson who was three months and three days old today. My son got up and switched on the lights to see what that child -- and I was sleeping in the other room. "Meanwhile, these HOS men -- no, not the HOS men but the HVO army came to the door, kicked the door off the hinges and immediately let off a burst of fire. They entered the room. The lights were on. They saw my son on his feet, so they immediately got him down. I was behind the door, and I was peering. Then they turned their weapons on my daughter-in-law and my other grandson. "Then they started but the little one was in the cradle and let out a sound, and then they returned, and one of the soldiers returned and fired the whole burst of fire into the small one in the cradle, the little one of three months and three days. "I tried to go there, but they immediately lighted two fires in that room and in the kitchen, so the fire spread very quickly. I tried to get those children to the other room where I was, and tried to localise the fire. I mean, they may have been killed but I hope I tried to save them from being burned down, but I fell completely because the flames were spreading frighteningly quickly. "I was sitting in the corner of that room and the window was open, and here the door had already burned down and the windows in that room where the children had been asleep."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you watch this carefully?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the news item that was broadcast that day when you watched the news on TV Sarajevo with Anto Rajic?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: Yes, but the last part is missing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is missing?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: Well, what's missing is when the journalist, whether he or she asks who did that and did he recognise who had done that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what you are claiming is that this cassette is not complete because the end is missing.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: Quite right. It is not complete.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you heard of a TV Sarajevo broadcast called "The Hague Diary"?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever seen that programme?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in this part of this story -- of [redacted] [redacted] story, did you take note of his mentioning that -- first saying that this was done HOS men and then immediately correcting himself and saying it was the HVO? Do you know what colour was the HOS uniform? If you know it, of course. If you don't, then that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of the Jokers?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: Yes, I have heard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, who were the Jokers?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: I don't know that either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what colour their uniform was?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever serving on village guards, you personally?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why was that?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: Because I had already been assigned to the anti-aircraft defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That PZO or AAD, was it established only after the elections.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: That is beforehand we called it PVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did it exist before?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: It existed before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, was that the mobilisation of anti-aircraft defence members when you joined this unit or how was it that you were activated?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: Well, it was on the 1st of June, '92. I was still -- that is when the Serb aircraft flew over.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This gun, Bofors, the 40 millimetre that you served, is it single barrelled or multi-barrelled?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: Its range is 9.000, and instantaneous four and a half.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what aircraft did it defend you effectively against? How should an aircraft fly that you can hit it with this particular gun?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: Why, that is something that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So tell us, can you hit a plane flying at an altitude of 10.000 metres?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: No, I could not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it's efficiency is limited by its limited range, if I understood it properly?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Counsel Radovic, I assume there is no cross-examination by other Defence counsel. Mr. Blaxill.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Cross-examined by Mr. Blaxill:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Safradin, good afternoon. My name is Michael Blaxill. I'm one of the Prosecution attorneys assigned to this case. As a result of what you've said to today I do have a few questions for you if you'll bear with me. I hope it will not take too long. You say that you were activated in service in June, 1992, is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go straight into service with an anti-aircraft unit?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your neighbour Mr. Anto Rajic also in that unit at that time?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: He was, yes, except that he was there before me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you joined were you, in fact, assigned to the same gun team as Mr. Rajic?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, in fact, was he your gun commander? He was your superior on that gun team?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would I be right in assuming, therefore, that every time that Mr. Rajic was on duty with the gun so you would you be? Did you work as a team all the time?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You had what, about three other team-mates to operate the gun? It's a five-man gun; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were serving after -- let us move on from June through July and August of 1992. Did you consider yourself, at that time, serving in the HVO or some organisation like that? Did you feel that your anti-aircraft unit formed part of such an organisation?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you consider your overall military structure to be then? What army did you belong to; if I can ask that.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: The anti-aircraft defence existed even before as the Territorial Defence, even while we were all together. So it all existed before, and we did not have anything, that is, we did not have any -- we did not belong to any command, the HVO or anything else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Later on, did that change at all? Did the TO and others share out the guns, and separate, and do different duty?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: Afterwards, afterwards, during the conflicts and suchlike, they separated. That is, some weapons went to the Muslim side and some stayed with us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About when do you remember that happening?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: It happened right after the -- or around the conflict, or in the wake of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which conflict are we referring to there, sir? Was that the one, the October '92?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: Yes, after the first conflict.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, on the 16th of April of 1993, your gun team was in -- and I hope -- is it Prahulje? My pronunciation is probably very poor. I apologise for that. Is that the village you were in on the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me which village you were in on the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: On the 16th, I was at home in the village of Santici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were home in the village of Santici. Were you therefore on leave from your military duty?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: Yes, and the 17th, I reported at Prahulje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So on the morning of the 16th, you were actually in Santici when the conflict started, or shooting was heard in Ahmici nearby, is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what did you do on the 16th? Since this conflict has started nearby, what did you do? Did you try and report somewhere?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: No, I did not. That day I spent at home. I did not report anywhere because I hoped that I would not have to report back at Prahulje earlier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, at your home in Santici, how far were you from the village of Ahmici, from where the shooting was going on?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: It's a kilometre, a kilometre and a half.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you feel at that time that you were safe where you were, in your home in Santici, and that your family was safe?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: Well, there was nothing --I mean, Santici is a Croatian village. There was nothing -- I mean, I was simply at home, and there were no problems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was a Croatian village, and there were no problems there; what made you then report for duty on the 17th of April?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: Because I was due on that date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In other words, that was your due date to return to your unit; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your decision to report in had nothing to do with the conflict going on relatively nearby in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You reported where on the 17th?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: I reported where I was assigned to be on duty, that is, at Prahulje, where the weapon was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that day, on that day you reported, did you just stay with your weapon for a period of time that day?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: I reported on the 17th, and I was there that day at night, and around noon on the 18th, we moved to a place called Pokrajcici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, on the night or early evening or the night of the 17th, did you leave your gun position and go to any accommodation for rest, to eat, to sleep?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: Yes, Anto Rajic and I went to my brother's, but we did not spend the night there. We went back again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you went to your brother's place for a period of time during that night, is that correct, and not the whole night?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: It was the evening of the 17th, and we did not spend the whole night. We went back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did your brother live?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Novi Travnik. How far was that from the gun position?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: It's about five or six kilometres, maybe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have a vehicle in which to travel?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: Well, we went there -- we had a vehicle. I can't really remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall, did your brother have a television?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: Sure, he had television, but we went up there because we needed more members of the team and since he was also a member of the anti-aircraft defence with us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But on your visit to his home, did you in fact watch any television?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you not curious about the recent events of the day before, the shooting you had heard in Ahmici? Were you not curious to try and catch up on the news?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: No, we did not. I think there was no electricity in Novi Travnik either. There was no electricity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You then returned to your gun position later that night, and I believe said you were transferred on the day of the 18th. Was that around noon, I believe you said?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was it you went on the 18th?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: We went to a locality, to a place called Pokrajcici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe there Mr. Rajic arranged for you to have some accommodation to stay in whilst you were there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: Well, we arrived in Pokrajcici, got put up there, and he and Ivan went to look for some accommodation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By that evening, you had accommodation arranged at the house of the family Bilic; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you clearly say you recalled seeing the interview that we have seen here on video, and that you knew [redacted] before because you had been to school with his son; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any other element of the news, though, that caught your interest in particular? Any news about Ahmici, Santici? These are close by you.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: No. I don't think I remember anything else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're saying the only element of the news that night that you recall was the interview of the gentleman, [redacted], from a hospital bed? That's what you're saying, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall any other programmes that were on the television that evening that may have been watched by yourself and Mr. Rajic?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Do you recall any other television programmes that came on in the course of that evening while you were watching television with Mr. Rajic at the Bilic household?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: I only watched the news, so that is the main news programme of the Sarajevo television which showed it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you -- I will just ask again: Have you ever seen that broadcast on any other time subsequent to the 18th of April, 1993, either on television or by way of a video recording, before today, have you ever seen it?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAFRADIN
utterances.text: After that, no, I did not see it again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, when you were aware of the accusation against Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic, these two gentlemen are known to you, are they?
